github.readme:
What is it?
Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, an open-weight, native multimodal agentic model. It is the first open 3T-class model, designed for frontier intelligence in long-horizon coding, knowledge work, and reasoning.

Problem solved
The model addresses the need for high-capacity agents that can sustain long engineering sessions with minimal human oversight. It navigates massive repositories and orchestrates complex terminal tools, from GPU kernel optimization to chip design, while supporting deep research with interactive visualizations.

How does it work?
Kimi K3 is a 2.8T-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 104B activated parameters. It utilizes Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes). The architecture features 93 layers, selecting 16 out of 896 experts. It employs a Stable LatentMoE framework and native MXFP4 quantization with MXFP8 activations.

Who should use it?
AI engineers, researchers, and technical product readers seeking open frontier weights for deployment. It is particularly suited for teams building agentic coding assistants and knowledge work applications requiring extensive context.

Why is it useful?
It offers approximately 2.5x scaling efficiency improvement over Kimi K2. The model supports a 1-million-token context window and native multimodality, handling text, images, and video within a single architecture. It preserves thinking history for multi-turn conversations and tool calls.

Key capabilities
Kimi K3 supports reasoning effort levels (low, high, max) and returns reasoning content. It integrates with vLLM, SGLang, and TokenSpeed. The model includes a 401M parameter MoonViT-V2 vision encoder and a 160K vocabulary.

Performance
Kimi K3 scores 93.5 on GPQA Diamond and 88.3 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. It achieves 91.2 on BrowseComp and 84.8 on OSWorld-Verified. In coding, it reaches 81.2 on FrontierSWE and 42.0 on SWE-Marathon.

Maturity/status
The model is production-ready with full weights released under the Kimi K3 License and available via API.

papers.title: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence
papers.description: We introduce Kimi K3, a 2.8T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 104 billion activated parameters, native vision capabilities, and a 1-million-token context window. Kimi K3 is built on Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals, which improve information flow across sequence length and model depth. Together with Stable LatentMoE, which effectively activates 16 of 896 routed experts per token, and refined training and data recipes, these advances yield an approximately 2.5x improvement in overall scaling efficiency over Kimi K2. Post-training highlights reinforcement learning across general, agentic, and coding domains and multiple reasoning-effort levels, enabling compositional generalization and robust long-horizon execution. At 2.8T scale, Kimi K3 is supported by infrastructure advances in multiple areas: algorithm-system co-design for KDA, perfectly balanced expert-parallel training with efficient memory management, million-token agentic RL with persistent rollout and sandbox states, and deployment innovations. Extensive evaluations show that Kimi K3 achieves frontier-level performance across long-horizon coding, agentic, knowledge, reasoning, and vision tasks. While its overall performance still trails the most powerful proprietary models, namely Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3 consistently outperforms other open and proprietary models evaluated in our suite. We release the full Kimi K3 model weights to facilitate future research and accelerate the broader deployment and adoption of frontier intelligence.

items.name: alibaba/open-code-review
items.reason: This item represents a significant development in AI engineering, combining a high-impact open-source tool with a peer-reviewed research paper. The hybrid architecture (deterministic pipelines + LLM agents) addresses critical industry pain points like hallucination and token costs, offering a practical alternative to purely generative approaches. With massive community adoption (42k+ stars), strong benchmark performance (2.17x SEM-F1 improvement), and backing by a major tech company, it is highly relevant for a technical audience focused on scalable AI integration.

github.description: Secure, fast, efficient, battle-tested at Alibaba's scale. Hybrid architecture code review tool: deterministic pipelines + LLM Agent, precise line-level comments, built-in multi-language ruleset (NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection), OpenAI & Anthropic compatible.
github.readme:
What is it?
OpenCodeReview is an AI-powered code review CLI tool incubated from Alibaba Group’s internal systems. It analyzes Git diffs to generate structured, line-level review comments. The tool is built for speed, security, and efficiency at massive scale.

Problem solved
General-purpose agents often suffer from incomplete coverage on large changesets, position drift in reported issues, and unstable quality due to prompt sensitivity. This project addresses these pain points by replacing purely language-driven approaches with a hybrid architecture that ensures consistency and precision.

How does it work?
The tool combines deterministic engineering with an LLM agent. Deterministic logic handles hard constraints like precise file selection, smart bundling of related files, and fine-grained rule matching. The agent performs dynamic decision-making using scenario-tuned prompts and a distilled toolset optimized for code review tasks.

Who should use it?
This tool is designed for developers and engineering teams seeking reliable automated code reviews. It supports integration with major coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Kimi Code, making it suitable for both individual contributors and large-scale enterprise environments.

Why is it useful?
It reduces false alarms and API costs while maintaining high accuracy. By separating deterministic checks from dynamic analysis, it delivers stable, predictable feedback that integrates seamlessly into existing CI/CD pipelines and local development workflows without requiring extensive configuration.

Key capabilities
It features built-in multi-language rulesets for detecting NPE, thread-safety, XSS, and SQL injection. The tool supports OpenAI and Anthropic compatible models, offers full-file scanning via `ocr scan`, and provides delegation modes for AI host agents.

Performance
Benchmarks on 200 real PRs show significantly higher precision and F1 scores compared to general-purpose agents. It consumes approximately one-ninth of the tokens while completing reviews faster, though with lower recall, a deliberate trade-off favoring precision.

Maturity/status
The project is battle-tested, having served tens of thousands of Alibaba developers and identified millions of defects over two years. It is now available as an open-source, production-ready tool.

papers.title: Automated Code Review in Practice
papers.description: Context: Code review is a widespread practice among practitioners to improve software quality and transfer knowledge. It is often perceived as time-consuming due to the need for manual effort and potential delays in the development process. Several AI-assisted code review tools (Qodo, GitHub Copilot, Coderabbit, etc.) provide automated code reviews using large language models (LLMs). The overall effects of such tools in the industry setting are yet to be examined. Objective: This study examines the impact of LLM-based automated code review tools in an industry setting. Method: The study was conducted within an industrial software development environment that adopted an AI-assisted code review tool (based on open-source Qodo PR Agent). 238 practitioners across ten projects had access to the tool. We focused our analysis on three projects, which included $\mathbf{4, 3 3 5}$ pull requests, 1,568 of which underwent automated reviews. Our data collection comprised three sources: (1) a quantitative analysis of pull request data, including comment labels indicating whether developers acted on the automated comments, (2) surveys sent to developers regarding their experience with the reviews on individual pull requests, and (3) a broader survey of 22 practitioners capturing their general opinions on automated code reviews. Results: $73.8\%$ of automated code review comments were labeled as resolved. However, the overall average pull request closure duration increased from five hours 52 minutes to eight hours 20 minutes, with varying trends observed across different projects. According to survey responses, most practitioners observed a minor improvement in code quality as a result of automated code reviews. Conclusion: The LLM-based automated code review tool proved useful in software development, enhancing bug detection, increasing awareness of code quality, and promoting best practices. However, it also led to longer pull request closure times and introduced drawbacks such as faulty reviews, unnecessary corrections, and irrelevant comments. Based on these findings, we discussed how practitioners can more effectively utilize automated code review technologies.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This study evaluates the real-world impact of LLM-based automated code review tools within an industrial software development environment. It analyzes data from practitioners using an open-source Qodo PR Agent to understand how automation affects workflow and code quality.

What the paper actually contributes.
The authors present empirical evidence on the adoption of AI-assisted code review, focusing on developer interaction with automated comments and the resulting changes in pull request dynamics.

Problem solved
Code review is often perceived as time-consuming and delayed due to manual effort. This research addresses the gap in understanding how AI tools actually perform in production settings, moving beyond theoretical benefits to practical outcomes.

How does it work?
The study analyzed 4,335 pull requests across three projects, with 1,568 undergoing automated reviews. Data sources included quantitative PR metrics, individual survey responses, and broader practitioner opinions from 22 developers.

Who should use it?
Software engineers, technical product managers, and researchers interested in AI-assisted development workflows and industrial software engineering practices.

Why is it useful?
It reveals that while automated reviews enhance bug detection and code quality awareness, they also increase closure times. This helps teams balance efficiency gains against potential workflow bottlenecks.

Key capabilities
The tool generated comments that were labeled for developer action. The analysis tracked resolution rates and developer sentiment regarding the relevance and accuracy of automated feedback.

Performance
Seventy-three point eight percent of automated comments were resolved. However, average pull request closure duration increased from five hours 52 minutes to eight hours 20 minutes.

Maturity/status
Peer-reviewed at the 2025 IEEE/ACM ICSE-SEIP conference.

papers.title: OpenCodeReview: Determinism over Non-Determinism for Cost-Effective Agent-Based Code Review
papers.description: LLM-based code review agents promise scalable, always-on review, yet current systems suffer from two intertwined weaknesses: (1) non-determinism--unbounded tool use makes review outcomes unstable, and (2) context locality--the reviewer's access remains bounded to the diff, capping discoverable issue depth. Both give rise to three challenges: misaligned context retrieval, a coherence-efficiency trade-off in multi-file pull requests, and hallucinated comments that erode trust. To address these, we introduce OpenCodeReview, built on deterministic engineering for uncertain agents: rather than granting maximal freedom, we inject determinism at three deliberate pipeline points. Rule-Guided Dispatch uses a multi-layer rule system to deterministically select files and review criteria, eliminating variability of agent-driven triage. Grounded File Review replaces free-form exploration with a curated tool set exposed through a ReAct loop, while file-level parallel SubAgents balance context coherence against efficiency and recover cross-file dependencies on demand. Independent Reflection introduces a falsification-first filter under an asymmetric information boundary--the reflector sees only the diff, not the agent's tool-augmented exploration--removing hallucinated comments without self-reinforcing bias, improving precision while preserving recall. On AACR-Bench (200 real-world PRs, 10 languages, 1,505 expert-verified comments), OpenCodeReview outperforms mainstream coding agents (e.g., Claude Code and Codex) across six LLM backends, achieving up to 2.17x higher SEM-F1 (25.10% vs. 11.57%) while consuming 5-15x fewer tokens. We open-source OpenCodeReview at https://github.com/alibaba/open-code-review.
papers.readme:
What is it?
OpenCodeReview is a deterministic agent framework for automated code review. It replaces non-deterministic LLM exploration with structured, rule-based pipelines to ensure stable and cost-effective outcomes.

Problem solved
Current LLM review agents suffer from unbounded tool use and limited context. This leads to unstable results, missed issues in multi-file pull requests, and hallucinated comments that erode developer trust.

How does it work?
The system injects determinism at three points. Rule-Guided Dispatch uses multi-layer rules to select files and criteria, eliminating triage variability. Grounded File Review employs a curated tool set via a ReAct loop, while parallel SubAgents balance coherence and efficiency. Independent Reflection uses a falsification-first filter where the reflector sees only the diff, removing hallucinations without self-reinforcing bias.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and technical product teams building scalable code review infrastructure. It is suitable for organizations prioritizing precision and cost control in automated software engineering workflows.

Why is it useful?
It significantly reduces token consumption while improving review quality. By enforcing deterministic paths, it provides reliable, always-on review capabilities that are more trustworthy than free-form agent approaches.

Key capabilities
The architecture integrates multi-layer rule systems, ReAct loops, and parallel sub-agents. It supports 10 programming languages and handles cross-file dependency recovery on demand.

Performance
On AACR-Bench, comprising 200 real-world pull requests and 1,505 expert-verified comments, OpenCodeReview achieves a 25.10% SEM-F1 score. This represents a 2.17x improvement over mainstream agents like Claude Code, while using 5-15x fewer tokens.

Maturity/status
The system is open-sourced on GitHub, indicating experimental availability for community adoption and further research.

items.name: jev llm
items.reason: The discovery highlights a significant shift towards non-generative, calibrated decision models (Jev) that offer superior cost and latency efficiency compared to LLMs for classification tasks. The combination of Nokia's open-source AnyJev library, recent academic analysis of the ecosystem, and benchmarking papers demonstrating performance parity with frontier models provides strong technical and practical value for AI engineers.

github.description: Turn any LLM into a Jev-style decision model: typed decisions, real probabilities, no training. (continue updating, welcome any issue and PR request)
github.readme:
What is it?
AnyJev transforms open LLMs into calibrated decision models without fine-tuning. It extracts typed choices with reliable probabilities from standard language models.

Problem solved
Raw logits suffer from position bias and poor calibration, making automated routing risky. Reordering options flips answers, and confidence scores are untrustworthy for thresholding.

How does it work?
The library uses three levels. L0 averages position bias via option rotation with zero labels. L1 applies temperature scaling using 100–500 labels. L2 fits a closed-form linear head on hidden states, requiring only 100–300 labels. It integrates with vLLM and transformers, serving decisions via pooling servers.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers building automated routing, classification, or decision systems. It suits teams needing calibrated probabilities from existing LLMs without training overhead.

Why is it useful?
It enables safe automation by providing trustworthy uncertainty estimates. You can set risk thresholds to route only high-confidence cases to automation, reducing human-in-the-loop costs while maintaining accuracy.

Key capabilities
Supports choice, yes/no, and score questions. Offers adaptive rotation budgets to reduce compute. Includes a self-maintaining head that adapts to rewordings using unlabelled traffic. Ships pre-fitted heads for Qwen3 models.

Performance
On Qwen3-8B with BANKING77, L0 reduces order-flip rate from 0.230 to 0.073. L2 achieves 0.771 accuracy with 0.095 calibration error. It allows 52.0% of traffic to be auto-decidable at 5% risk, up from 7.7% for raw logits.

Maturity/status
The project is an active research tool with Apache-2.0 licensing. It includes comprehensive benchmarks and is suitable for experimental deployment in production environments requiring calibrated outputs.

papers.title: Jev in the Wild: A Data-Driven Analysis of the Jev Model's Functionality, Applications and Ecosystem
papers.description: Jev is a fast, low-cost decision model that answers natural-language questions with choices, binary judgments, and scores. As its public ecosystem grows rapidly, it remains unclear how Jev is used across applications and how public attention relates to project distribution. To answer these questions, we conduct a large-scale, data-driven analysis of 2,170 publicly available Jev projects collected from GitHub as of September 22, 2026. We find rapid early growth in Jev's public ecosystem, with both new projects and integration into existing repositories. Across diverse domains, projects use Jev for multiple decision purposes and combine its interfaces. Attribute judgment and scoring are widely used, while the use of action selection, content filtering, and model and tool selection varies across domains. These patterns suggest that Jev serves as a reusable decision component whose functionality varies with the surrounding workflow. Meanwhile, public attention is concentrated in routing and interface agents and does not track project counts. Our findings provide a quantitative view of Jev's emerging ecosystem and inform the design and evaluation of general-purpose decision models across diverse application contexts.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This paper analyzes the Jev model, a fast, low-cost decision engine designed to answer natural-language queries with choices, binary judgments, and scores. The study examines its growing public ecosystem to understand real-world usage patterns.

What the paper actually contributes.
The authors present a large-scale, data-driven analysis of 2,170 publicly available Jev projects collected from GitHub as of September 22, 2026. They map how Jev integrates into existing repositories and diverse application domains.

Problem solved.
As Jev’s public ecosystem expands rapidly, it remains unclear how the model is utilized across different applications. This research addresses the gap in understanding the relationship between public attention and actual project distribution.

How does it work?
The team conducted a quantitative analysis of the GitHub dataset to identify usage trends. They categorized projects by decision purpose, noting that attribute judgment and scoring are widely adopted. The study highlights how Jev functions as a reusable component within varied workflows.

Who should use it?
AI engineers, researchers, and technical product readers interested in decision models and ecosystem analysis. The findings inform the design and evaluation of general-purpose decision models.

Why is it useful?
The study provides a quantitative view of Jev’s emerging ecosystem. It reveals that public attention concentrates in routing and interface agents rather than tracking project counts. This data helps developers understand practical integration patterns.

Key capabilities.
Jev supports multiple decision purposes including action selection, content filtering, and model selection. These capabilities vary across domains, allowing the model to adapt to surrounding workflow requirements effectively.

papers.title: Decision Without Generation: Benchmarking a Calibrated Non-Generative Decision Model Against LLM Judges on Moderation, Hallucination, NLI and Prompt-Injection Tasks
papers.description: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as judges for content moderation, hallucination detection and prompt-injection filtering, although they are slow, expensive and poorly calibrated when asked to verbalise probabilities. We evaluate a different design point: a commercially served decision-only model (typesafe/jev-1.13, "Jev") that returns a typed, calibrated decision for a narrow input and is billed on input tokens only. On identical items from seven public benchmarks (ToxicChat, BeaverTails, HaluEval-QA/Dialogue, BoolQ, ANLI-R3, a prompt-injection set; n=500-600 each, with Jev replicated on complete splits, 54,634 decisions), Jev has the highest AUROC of any cheap-tier LLM (GPT-5.4-nano, GPT-5-mini, Claude Haiku 4.5) on all six binary tasks, ties Haiku on ANLI, and is never significantly worse than a cheap-tier model under paired bootstrap, at 3-63x lower cost and 3.7-8.6x lower latency. Against frontier models run as equal-cost classifiers, Jev is significantly better than GPT-5.4 (reasoning off) on 4 tasks and tied on 3, one of which (HaluEval-QA, -0.013 AUROC) is a borderline loss; Claude Sonnet 4.6 (42-97x the cost) beats Jev on ANLI-R3 and dialogue-grounded hallucination. Jev's raw probabilities have lower Brier than every LLM's; after cross-fitted Platt recalibration the gap persists against the cheap tier and GPT-5.4 but closes against Sonnet. A quantisation control shows the ranking advantage is not an artefact of the LLMs' coarser verbalised probabilities. We report a negative result - no cheap-tier cascade on Jev's uncertain band significantly improves on Jev alone - and two self-caught evaluation artefacts. Principal limitations: public benchmarks that the model may have seen in training; a single-vendor black box; no same-item specialist classifier baselines. Technical report (preprint), version 1.0.0. Generative AI use: Fable 5.1 was used for manuscript drafting and experimental code generation. OpenAI Codex assisted with preparing the public release, documenting the repository and checking offline reproducibility of the archived numerical results. The author takes responsibility for the report and its results. Author affiliation: Canly Inc.; Chief AI Officer (CAIO). Correspondence: hagino@apache.org. papers.readme:
What is it?
This paper evaluates Jev, a non-generative decision model, against large language models used as judges for moderation and safety tasks.

What the paper actually contributes.
It benchmarks a typed, calibrated decision model against cheap and frontier LLMs on seven public benchmarks. The study includes 54,634 replicated decisions to assess accuracy, calibration, and cost efficiency.

Problem solved
LLMs are slow, expensive, and poorly calibrated when asked to verbalise probabilities for binary classification tasks. This work addresses the need for faster, cheaper alternatives that maintain high reliability.

How does it work?
The authors test typesafe/jev-1.13, a commercially served model billed on input tokens only. It returns typed decisions without generation. The evaluation uses paired bootstrap tests and Platt recalibration to compare performance against models like GPT-5.4-nano and Claude Haiku 4.5.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers focused on cost-effective content moderation, hallucination detection, and prompt-injection filtering.

Why is it useful?
Jev achieves the highest AUROC among cheap-tier LLMs across six binary tasks. It operates at 3-63x lower cost and 3.7-8.6x lower latency than comparable models. Raw probabilities show lower Brier scores than all LLMs, indicating superior calibration.

Key capabilities
The model is evaluated on ToxicChat, BeaverTails, HaluEval-QA/Dialogue, BoolQ, ANLI-R3, and a prompt-injection set. Each dataset contains 500-600 items. The study also reports a negative result regarding cascades on Jev’s uncertain band.

Performance
Jev significantly outperforms GPT-5.4 (reasoning off) on four tasks and ties on three. It is never significantly worse than any cheap-tier model. Claude Sonnet 4.6 beats Jev only on ANLI-R3 and dialogue-grounded hallucination.

Maturity/status
This is a technical report and preprint hosted on Zenodo. It is version 1.0.0 with an open software archive.

papers.title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling
papers.description: Control evaluations measure whether monitoring and security protocols for AI systems prevent intentionally subversive AI models from causing harm. Our work presents the first control evaluation performed in an agent environment. We construct BashBench, a dataset of 257 challenging multi-step system administration tasks, and evaluate whether various safety measures can prevent an adversarially constructed AI agent from covertly downloading and executing malicious code in this environment. This multi-step setting introduces new attack and defense dynamics, which we investigate in order to design novel control protocols that prevent safety failures without hindering the ability of non-malicious agents to perform useful work. We introduce a class of control protocols called resample protocols that dynamically take additional samples of certain actions. We find these protocols significantly improve on existing techniques by selectively blocking the AI agent from executing suspicious code and incriminating the agent by generating additional examples of dangerous behavior. We measure the tradeoff between attack prevention and usefulness; our best protocol combines resampling with analysis of previous steps, reducing the success rate of attacks from 58% to 7% at a 5% cost to the performance of a non-malicious agent.
papers.readme:
What is it?

Problem solved

How does it work?
The authors propose resample protocols that dynamically take additional samples of specific actions to detect suspicious behavior. They combine this with analysis of previous steps to incriminate agents exhibiting dangerous patterns. This approach allows for selective blocking of threats while preserving the utility of non-malicious tasks.

Who should use it?

papers.title: MalSkillBench: A Runtime-Verified Benchmark of Malicious Agent Skills
papers.description:
AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Gemini CLI increasingly extend themselves with third-party skills: markdown packages bundling natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and tool permissions. Because a skill is at once code and agent-facing instruction, it introduces a supply chain dependency whose risk is neither pure code nor pure prompt. Detection tools have never been measured against verified ground truth spanning this hybrid space, leaving their effectiveness unknown and wild-only evaluations biased.
  We present MalSkillBench, the first runtime-verified benchmark of malicious agent skills: 3,944 malicious skills labeled along a three-dimensional taxonomy of 108 cells. Of these, 3,214 come from a closed-loop Generate-Verify-Feedback pipeline admitting only samples whose malicious behavior fires inside a Docker sandbox under system-call monitoring and an LLM judge; we add 703 in-the-wild and 4,000 matched benign skills. Our measurements are consistent: code injection reaches 94.5% verification yield but prompt injection only 75.8%, the same fragility that later makes it hard to detect; the wild sample is narrow, dominated by one cryptocurrency-theft campaign (86.6% one behavior, 81% from two accounts) with a small but architecturally new tail attacking the agent control plane; the strongest skill-specific detector reaches 98.4% recall on code injection yet collapses on prompt-injection and agent-control attacks, and wild-only scoring swings the ranking by up to 66 recall points; supply-chain scanners and prompt-injection defenses each see only half of a skill, and no combination recovers the code-instruction relationship. Detecting malicious skills therefore requires reasoning jointly over task intent, code, and instructions. We release the dataset, pipeline, baselines, and results.

What is it?

Problem solved
Current detection tools lack measured effectiveness against verified ground truth. Existing evaluations are biased by wild-only samples that miss the supply chain nuances of agent-facing instructions.

How does it work?
The dataset contains 3,944 malicious skills labeled across a three-dimensional taxonomy of 108 cells. The authors add 703 in-the-wild skills and 4,000 matched benign skills to the collection.

AI engineering teams and security researchers building defenses for autonomous coding agents.

No single detector works; the strongest skill-specific tool hits 98.4% recall on code injection but collapses on prompt injection. Supply-chain scanners miss half the skill, proving joint reasoning over intent, code, and instructions is essential.

Key capabilities

Performance
Wild-only scoring swings rankings by up to 66 recall points.

github.description: A coding-agent skill for multi-phase security audits with independently verified, machine-readable findings
github.readme:
What is it?
This repository provides a coding-agent skill that transforms automated assistants into rigorous security auditors. It enables multi-phase security reviews with independently verified, machine-readable findings. The project originated from Cloudflare’s internal vulnerability discovery harness, representing a distilled, single-repo starting point for that evolved system.

Problem solved
Traditional automated scans often miss complex logic flaws or produce false positives. This tool addresses the need for structured, evidence-based auditing that distinguishes between confirmed vulnerabilities, unverified leads, and disproved candidates. It ensures that findings are grounded in actual source code behavior rather than static analysis heuristics.

How does it work?
The skill orchestrates isolated agents through six distinct phases: reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting. It maintains a `coverage-ledger.json` to track architectural trust boundaries and input surfaces. Unique candidates undergo adversarial validation by fresh agents to disprove them. Zero-dependency Node.js scripts validate the JSON schema for findings and coverage data at each stage.

Who should use it?
AI engineers, security researchers, and technical product managers building or integrating autonomous coding agents. It requires a coding agent supporting tool use and parallel sub-agents. Teams must also enforce OS-level sandboxes with network isolation and resource limits to safely execute target-controlled builds and tests.

Why is it useful?
It enforces strict verification protocols, ensuring severity ratings reflect actual impact rather than checklist deviations. Multiple additive runs improve coverage, with tests showing repeated audits find significantly more vulnerabilities than single passes. The structured output facilitates integration into existing DevSecOps pipelines via standardized JSON and Markdown reports.

Key capabilities
The system supports diverse attack classes including memory safety, LLM prompt injection, web protocols, supply chain risks, and cloud deployment configurations. It generates detailed reports like `REPORT.md` and `FINDINGS-DETAIL.md`. Installation is handled via the Skills CLI, allowing global or local deployment within agent workflows.

papers.title: SkillProbe: Security Auditing for Emerging Agent Skill Marketplaces via Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.description: With the rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) agent ecosystems, centralized skill marketplaces have emerged as pivotal infrastructure for augmenting agent capabilities. However, these marketplaces face unprecedented security challenges, primarily stemming from semantic-behavioral inconsistency and inter-skill combinatorial risks, where individually benign skills induce malicious behaviors during collaborative invocation. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose SkillProbe, a multi-stage security auditing framework driven by multi-agent collaboration. SkillProbe introduces a"Skills-for-Skills"design paradigm, encapsulating auditing processes into standardized skill modules to drive specialized agents through a rigorous pipeline, including admission filtering, semantic-behavioral alignment detection, and combinatorial risk simulation. We conducted a large-scale evaluation using 8 mainstream LLM series across 2,500 real-world skills from ClawHub. Our results reveal a striking popularity-security paradox, where download volume is not a reliable proxy for security quality, as over 90% of high-popularity skills failed to pass rigorous auditing. Crucially, we discovered that high-risk skills form a single giant connected component within the risk-link dimension, demonstrating that cascaded risks are systemic rather than isolated occurrences. We hope that SkillProbe will inspire researchers to provide a scalable governance infrastructure for constructing a trustworthy Agentic Web. SkillProbe is accessible for public experience at skillhub.holosai.io.

github.readme:
What is it?
Qwen-Image-2.1 is a unified 7B-parameter open-source text-to-image and image editing model. It balances generation quality with inference efficiency using a compact visual generation component.

Problem solved
It addresses the need for a single model handling both creation and editing tasks. It specifically targets pain points in maintaining identity across multiple references and generating transparent backgrounds without separate tools.

How does it work?
The architecture uses a single-stream DiT with 32 layers and mixed-granularity attention. It employs a Qwen3-VL 8B text encoder and a 64-channel RGBA VAE. Prefix KV cache reuse accelerates editing by caching condition images and text instructions across denoising steps.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers seeking efficient, high-quality image generation. Developers building applications requiring native transparency or multi-reference composition will find this model directly applicable to their workflows.

Why is it useful?
It reduces computational costs while delivering realistic textures and refined aesthetics. The native RGBA support eliminates post-processing steps for transparent assets, streamlining production pipelines for designers and developers.

Key capabilities
The model supports up to 10 reference images for composition. It enables local edits via circles, painted annotations, or masks. It generates 2K resolution images natively and preserves identity for people and products.

Performance
No specific benchmark scores are provided in the README.

papers.title: Qwen-Image-2.0 Technical Report
papers.description: We present Qwen-Image-2.0, an omni-capable image generation foundation model that unifies high-fidelity generation and precise image editing within a single framework. Despite recent progress, existing models still struggle with ultra-long text rendering, multilingual typography, high-resolution photorealism, robust instruction following, and efficient deployment, especially in text-rich and compositionally complex scenarios. Qwen-Image-2.0 addresses these challenges by coupling Qwen3-VL as the condition encoder with a Multimodal Diffusion Transformer for joint condition-target modeling, supported by large-scale data curation and a customized multi-stage training pipeline. This enables strong multimodal understanding while preserving flexible generation and editing capabilities. The model supports instructions of up to 1K tokens for generating text-rich content such as slides, posters, infographics, and comics, while significantly improving multilingual text fidelity and typography. It also enhances photorealistic generation with richer details, more realistic textures, and coherent lighting, and follows complex prompts more reliably across diverse styles. Extensive human evaluations show that Qwen-Image-2.0 substantially outperforms previous Qwen-Image models in both generation and editing, marking a step toward more general, reliable, and practical image generation foundation models.

papers.title: Beyond the Prompt: Gender Bias in Text-to-Image Models, with a Case Study on Hospital Professions
papers.description: Text-to-image (TTI) models are increasingly used in professional, educational, and creative contexts, yet their outputs often embed and amplify social biases. This paper investigates gender representation in six state-of-the-art open-weight models: HunyuanImage 2.1, HiDream-I1-dev, Qwen-Image, FLUX.1-dev, Stable-Diffusion 3.5 Large, and Stable-Diffusion-XL. Using carefully designed prompts, we generated 100 images for each combination of five hospital-related professions (cardiologist, hospital director, nurse, paramedic, surgeon) and five portrait qualifiers ("", corporate, neutral, aesthetic, beautiful). Our analysis reveals systematic occupational stereotypes: all models produced nurses exclusively as women and surgeons predominantly as men. However, differences emerge across models: Qwen-Image and SDXL enforce rigid male dominance, HiDream-I1-dev shows mixed outcomes, and FLUX.1-dev skews female in most roles. HunyuanImage 2.1 and Stable-Diffusion 3.5 Large also reproduce gender stereotypes but with varying degrees of sensitivity to prompt formulation. Portrait qualifiers further modulate gender balance, with terms like corporate reinforcing male depictions and beautiful favoring female ones. Sensitivity varies widely: Qwen-Image remains nearly unaffected, while FLUX.1-dev, SDXL, and SD3.5 show strong prompt dependence. These findings demonstrate that gender bias in TTI models is both systematic and model-specific. Beyond documenting disparities, we argue that prompt wording plays a critical role in shaping demographic outcomes. The results underscore the need for bias-aware design, balanced defaults, and user guidance to prevent the reinforcement of occupational stereotypes in generative AI.

papers.title: MCP in the Wild: Cross-Domain Knowledge Discovery through Multi-Server Orchestration
papers.description: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how large language model (LLM) agents discover and invoke external tools. Over 50 academic papers have evaluated MCP in single-server settings; none examine multi-server composition for cross-domain tasks. We present two complementary experiments. First, we execute 17 real MCP tool calls across 6 servers (arXiv, PubMed, Firecrawl, Context7, Memory, Filesystem) in 3 cross-domain case studies, producing 9 insights impossible within any single source and a 14-entity knowledge graph. Second, we benchmark cross-domain synthesis quality across 7 LLMs (GPT-5.4, DeepSeek R1, Mistral Large 3, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5) given identical MCP-collected data, achieving 100% task completion with significant variation in knowledge graph richness (3-15 entities). All seven models independently identified the same research gap, which we term the mechanism-pattern gap: frameworks provide multi-server connectivity mechanisms, but no prior work documents composition patterns for effective multi-server orchestration. We contribute a taxonomy of five composition patterns, all observed in practice, along with a failure taxonomy and design principles.
papers.readme:
What is it?
Dogan examines the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for multi-server orchestration, moving beyond standard single-server evaluations. The study investigates how LLM agents can combine tools across diverse domains to solve complex tasks.

What the paper actually contributes.
The author provides a taxonomy of five practical composition patterns for multi-server orchestration. Additionally, the work introduces a failure taxonomy and specific design principles for building robust cross-domain agent systems.

Problem solved.
Prior research evaluated MCP only in single-server settings. This work addresses the lack of documentation on composition patterns for effective multi-server orchestration, identifying a critical "mechanism-pattern gap" in current frameworks.

How does it work?
The study executes 17 real MCP tool calls across six servers: arXiv, PubMed, Firecrawl, Context7, Memory, and Filesystem. These calls were applied in three cross-domain case studies to synthesize knowledge and build entity graphs.

Who should use it?
AI engineers, researchers, and technical product readers building LLM agents that require cross-domain data synthesis and multi-tool integration.

Why is it useful?
The experiments produced nine insights impossible within any single source. It offers concrete patterns for orchestrating multiple MCP servers, helping developers avoid common failure modes in complex agent workflows.

Key capabilities.
The approach integrates academic databases, web scraping, memory, and filesystem tools. It generates 14-entity knowledge graphs from the collected data, enabling rich cross-domain knowledge discovery.

Performance.
Seven LLMs (GPT-5.4, DeepSeek R1, Mistral Large 3, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5) achieved 100% task completion. However, knowledge graph richness varied significantly, containing between three and fifteen entities.

Maturity/status.
The paper was published in 2026 by Elsevier BV, indicating peer-reviewed academic status.

items.name: obra/superpowers
items.reason: The repository exhibits exceptional momentum and community adoption, evidenced by nearly 300k stars and rapid growth in late 2025/2026. It addresses a critical pain point in AI agent development (planning and discipline) with broad compatibility across major coding agents. While it is primarily an engineering framework/prompt methodology rather than a novel architectural breakthrough, its immediate utility and impact on current AI workflows make it highly relevant for a technical audience.

github.description: An agentic skills framework & software development methodology that works.
github.readme:
What is it?
Superpowers is a composable skills framework and software development methodology designed to structure the behavior of coding agents. It provides a standardized set of instructions and plugins that guide AI agents through disciplined engineering workflows.

Problem solved
It addresses the tendency of coding agents to jump straight into implementation without proper planning, leading to context loss, redundant work, and poor code quality. The framework enforces a structured approach to ensure agents produce reliable, testable, and well-documented software.

How does it work?
The system activates automatically via a `using-superpowers` bootstrap hook in supported coding harnesses. It initiates a Socratic brainstorming phase to refine specifications before generating detailed implementation plans. The core execution utilizes subagent-driven development, where independent agents handle tasks with parallel reviews, enforcing strict test-driven development and systematic debugging protocols.

Who should use it?
The project targets AI engineers, technical product managers, and developers using major coding agents. It supports Claude Code, Codex App, Cursor, Devin CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, Grok Build CLI, Kimi Code, OpenCode, Pi, Qwen Code, Hermes Agent, and Muse.

Why is it useful?
Superpowers ensures agents follow consistent engineering practices like YAGNI, DRY, and red-green TDD. It reduces token waste by keeping agents on plan and allows for autonomous work sessions lasting hours. A diagnostic skill helps resolve session misbehavior by analyzing transcripts for errors.

Key capabilities
Features include brainstroming for design refinement, git worktree management for parallel branches, and subagent dispatching for concurrent task execution. It integrates with various plugin marketplaces and includes a telemetry feature to track version usage without exposing project data.

Maturity/status
The project is an open-source MIT-licensed framework with commercial support available for enterprise needs.

papers.title: Introducing Consort: A Spec-First Agent Framework for Enforced, Test-Driven Development on Live Database Branches
papers.description: When an agent writes code, the development framework becomes the control system for a non-deterministic worker. Spec-first, agent-driven frameworks have gained rapid traction since 2025; the installable ones, GitHub Spec Kit, obra/superpowers, BMAD, and GSD, and our own, all capture intent through a specification or durable planning artifacts. Since they agree on capturing intent up front, what separates them is how each enforces the engineering discipline that keeps agent-written code clean, correct, and maintainable. Every framework enforces that discipline somehow; they differ in how. We characterize three modes: enforcement by persuasion (prompt discipline the model may ignore), by front-loaded structure (strong specs, then a trusted build), and through controls the agent cannot edit (a deterministic orchestrator, human-approved gates, immutable tests, and a green result that must pass against a live, branched database). We introduce Consort, a spec-first, test-driven agent framework built on the third, enforcing that discipline through controls the agent runs inside but cannot bypass, in which a deterministic orchestrator drives separate role agents through a spec-first design lane and a test-driven build lane on a live database branch. We argue that enforcing the tests and gates in code keeps agent-written code honest and verifiable, while its specialized roles, like the human roles before them, are what make it maintainable, claims we frame as a pre-registered, testable hypothesis.
papers.readme:
What is it?
Consort is a spec-first, test-driven agent framework that enforces engineering discipline through immutable controls. It operates on the premise that deterministic orchestrators must drive role-based agents to ensure code integrity.

What the paper actually contributes.
The author introduces Consort as a system where a deterministic orchestrator manages separate role agents through distinct design and build lanes. The framework treats the development environment as a control system for non-deterministic workers, enforcing discipline via gates the agent cannot bypass.

Problem solved
Current spec-first frameworks rely on persuasion or front-loaded structure, which models may ignore. Consort addresses the gap in enforcing engineering discipline by ensuring agent-written code remains clean, correct, and maintainable through strict, uneditable controls rather than prompt-based suggestions.

How does it work?
Consort utilizes a deterministic orchestrator to drive role agents through a spec-first design lane and a test-driven build lane. It operates on live database branches, requiring green test results against a branched database. The architecture separates roles to mimic human organizational structures, ensuring maintainability.

Who should use it?
This framework targets AI engineers, researchers, and technical product readers interested in agent-driven development. It is particularly relevant for teams seeking to enforce strict engineering standards in automated code generation workflows.

Why is it useful?
Enforcing tests and gates in code keeps agent-written code honest and verifiable. The specialized roles ensure maintainability, framing these benefits as a pre-registered, testable hypothesis for future validation.

Key capabilities
The system integrates with live database branches and employs immutable tests. It features a deterministic orchestrator and separate role agents for design and build phases, ensuring human-approved gates are respected.

Performance
No specific benchmark scores are provided in the abstract.

Maturity/status
The venue is listed as not available, indicating an early-stage or preprint status.
